I’ve been off for about three months, maybe a bit more. It started when I got this surge of energy—like I didn’t need sleep. I was grading papers all night, then showing up early to teach with these grand plans to redesign the entire curriculum. I felt unstoppable. But then things… twisted. I started seeing shadows in the classroom when no one was there—figures in the corner, sometimes faces staring at me from the hallway. I knew they weren’t real, but they felt real.  

Then came the paranoia. I became convinced the school administration was bugging my room, that they were part of a group monitoring me for some larger experiment. I stopped using the office, avoided staff meetings—felt like every decision was being used against me.  

My body… sometimes I’d just lock up. Standing at the whiteboard, arm raised, and I couldn’t move it. A student once asked if I was okay, but I was frozen. Like my body wasn’t mine.  

But here’s the thing—the voices, the fear, the stiffness—they only happen when I’m in this wired, hyper state. Before that, I’m flat. After it passes, I crash hard. The psychosis doesn’t float on its own. It rides with the mania.
D005-D010_h022.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
D005-D010_h022.answer: C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D005-D010_h023.question:
I’ve been feeling on top of the world for the past couple of months—like I don’t need sleep, and my ideas are unstoppable. At the hospital, I’ve been bouncing between patients, talking a mile a minute, convinced I’m about to revolutionize surgery with these… grand, brilliant ideas. I barely sleep, maybe two hours a night, but I feel *electric*. That’s when the other things start.

There’s this nurse—I don’t even know her name, really—but I *know* she’s in love with me. She sends me coded messages through how she arranges the IV trays. Once, I tasted blood when I was just drinking water, and I swore it was a sign—like she was sending me messages through my senses. I laughed uncontrollably in the break room, making silly faces, playing with surgical gloves like puppets. My attending pulled me aside, concerned.

The mania’s been going strong for about three months now, and the voices, the tastes, the delusions—they only happen when I’m like this. When I crash, they’re gone. But right now? I’ve never felt more awake, more *seen*.
D005-D010_h023.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
D005-D010_h023.answer: C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D005-D010_h024.question:
I’m a jewelry designer, and honestly, the past few months have wrecked everything. My shop hasn’t opened in weeks. I used to lose myself in sketching designs, but now I can’t even hold a tool—my hands feel like they’re crawling with wires being threaded under my skin, like someone’s implanting devices. I know it sounds extreme, but I *feel* it. And I know the lab techs from my old supplier are watching me—cameras in the metal polishers, I think. That’s why I won’t go back.

But before all this… I wasn’t like this. I was *on*, nonstop. For over a week, I barely slept—didn’t need to. I was sketching 40 designs a night, convinced I was reinventing fine jewelry, that luxury stores across the world were waiting for my collection. I maxed out credit cards on materials, didn’t eat properly, snapped at clients. That’s when the sensations started—the touching, the whispers under my skin—and the ideas about being watched. But since then? No more energy. I just sit. When my assistant calls, I don’t answer. Not because I don’t care, but because it all feels pointless now.

The paranoia and the sensations? They didn’t come until that wild, sleepless time. And now that the drive’s gone, those things are fading too, though the fear lingers.
D005-D010_h024.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
D005-D010_h024.answer: C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D005-D010_h025.question:
I’ve been the head nurse at a busy city hospital for twelve years—juggling shifts, managing staff, managing my teenage daughter alone since the divorce. But about four months ago, something shifted. It started with energy—too much energy. I wasn’t sleeping more than two hours a night, but I felt sharp, unstoppable. I took on extra shifts, reorganized entire units, talked so fast my team could barely follow. That’s when the smells began. I kept smelling something burning, like rotting meat, but no one else did. I checked my scrubs, the break room, even the ambulance bay. Nothing.

Then I became convinced something was wrong with my liver—like it was decaying inside me. I asked the lab for blood tests every day. I’d stand in front of the mirror, prodding my abdomen, certain I could feel it swelling. At work, I started wearing gloves constantly, snapping them extra loud, arranging pens just so—little rituals, like if I didn’t do them right, everything would collapse.

But here’s the thing—those smells, the beliefs about my body, the odd habits—they only came during that intense high spell. Now that the energy’s faded, the voices and smells are gone too. I wasn’t like this before the episode, and not like this since.
D005-D010_h025.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
D005-D010_h025.answer: C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
